contributions.headingText: Primary CNS T-cell and NK/T-cell lymphomas are groups of malignant non-Hodgkin lymphomas, including peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL) and NK/T-cell lymphoma (nasal type), with primary manifestation in the CNS.
2B2Z Mature T-cell or NK-cell neoplasms, unspecified

In a series of 45 patients with primary CNS T-cell lymphoma, 19% had positive cerebrospinal fluid cytology, 4% had eye involvement, and 29% had multiple brain lesions {15800313; 26379152}.

Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma usually forms a single mass, but it may also occur with multiple lesions {20845062; 28342197}. Involved sites include the frontal and temporal lobes, cerebellum, pituitary {28342197; 29063643}, and (rarely) the leptomeninges {28222909}.

Patients with primary CNS T-cell lymphoma are adults aged 21–81 years (median: sixth decade), with an M:F ratio of about 1.5:1 {26379152}. Patients present with headache, neurological decline, seizures, and abnormalities of sensory and/or motor function {26379152; 26804925}.

Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma of the CNS affects patients aged 21–77 years (median: fifth decade), with a male preponderance (M:F ratio: ~2:1) {28342197}. Patients present with symptoms that are often rapidly progressive, including dizziness, headache, vomiting {20845062}, weakness, paralysis, aphasia {24419127}, dysphagia, dysarthria {29063643}, and mental deterioration {23279449}. Manifestations can mimic a cerebrovascular accident {23279449; 24419127}.

PTCLs accounted for 2–4% of primary CNS lymphomas in a European series {12525518}, and as many as 17% of primary CNS lymphomas in an Asian series {12826884}. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma is rare. Most reported patients were Asian {20845062; 23279449; 28342197; 29063643}; rarely, patients were African-American {24419127; 28342197} or Hispanic {28342197}.

Rare T-cell lymphomas {20975881} and one extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma {17899696} of the CNS have been reported in HIV-positive patients, and one CNS NK/T-cell lymphoma has been reported in a transplant recipient {28342197}, suggesting that immunodeficiency might play a role in the etiology of the disease in a subset of patients. One patient with a CD4-positive primary CNS T-cell lymphoma was seropositive for HTLV-1 {22118868}.
Mutations of DNMT3A, TET2, and several JAK/STAT pathway genes have been found in a subset of cases {26379152}.
Necrosis is common in extranodal NK/T-cell lymphomas {20845062; 28342197} and T-cell lymphomas {26379152}.

Most T-cell lymphomas in the CNS are PTCL-NOS {26379152; 26804925}. A minority of tumours (17% in one series) are anaplastic large cell lymphoma (see section Anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALK+/ALK−)) {26379152}. Most tumours in PTCL-NOS are composed of small and/or medium-sized atypical lymphoid cells; a minority are composed of medium-sized to large cells or mainly of large cells {12826884; 15725082; 18196250; 26379152}. PTCL often shows a prominent perivascular growth pattern and areas of necrosis {12826884; 15725082; 15800313; 18196250; 26379152}. Tumours are accompanied by reactive gliosis and a histiocytic reaction, but plasma cells, neutrophils, and eosinophils are usually inconspicuous {18196250; 26379152}.

Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphomas are composed of medium-sized, medium-sized and large, or large atypical, pleomorphic lymphoid cells with irregular nuclei (featuring dark or coarse chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli) and a moderate amount of pale cytoplasm {20845062; 23279449; 28342197}, accompanied by vascular proliferation and histiocytic infiltrates {29063643}. Mitotic figures are readily found, and angiocentric growth and extensive necrosis are common {28342197}. Necrosis is coagulative and apoptotic bodies are also seen {29063643}. A single case of a collision tumour with meningioma has been reported {30144614}.

Immunophenotype

Neoplastic cells in CNS PTCL are usually CD3-positive and CD56-negative; CD8 is expressed more often than CD4 {26379152}. Most tumours are of αβ T-cell lineage, but γδ lineage has been documented in a few cases {26379152; 26804925}. They typically express one or more cytotoxic granule proteins (TIA1, granzyme B, and/or perforin). CD2, CD5, and CD7 are each lost in subsets of cases {26379152}. Proliferation index is usually > 50% {26379152}. A case with aberrant coexpression of CD20 and CD79a has been reported {28612664}.

Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma is usually positive for CD3, CD56, cytotoxic granule protein, and EBV-encoded small RNA (EBER), and negative for CD5 and B-cell antigens {28342197}. Occasional cases express CD5 or lack CD56 {23279449; 28342197}. CD30 may be expressed {29063643}. A single case showed aberrant CD20 expression {29063643}.

Differential diagnosis

The differential diagnosis of T-cell lymphoma often includes a reactive inflammatory process because of the often relatively small size of tumour cells {26379152; 28612664}. Pan–T-cell antigen loss and clonal TR favour a PTCL; a polymorphous infiltrate with admixed inflammatory cells favours a reactive process {18196250; 26379152; 28612664}.

The differential diagnosis of NK/T-cell lymphoma includes B-cell lymphoma, especially lymphomatoid granulomatosis, because of the angiocentric growth and necrosis. Immunohistochemistry distinguishes the two entities. If the biopsy mainly shows necrosis, an infectious lesion can be considered in the differential diagnosis.
Cerebrospinal fluid involvement is reported in extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma with leptomeningeal disease; involvement can be documented by cytology augmented by flow cytometry {28222909}.

Clonal rearrangement of TR genes can be demonstrated in most T-cell lymphomas {26379152; 28612664}. In extranodal NK/T-cell lymphomas, TR genes are usually in germline configuration, but they may be clonally rearranged {20845062; 23279449}.
Staging is required to exclude a systemic primary; for cases of extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma in particular, the possibility of an occult primary in the upper respiratory tract should be excluded.

The outcome for patients with CNS T-cell lymphoma appears similar to that for patients with primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the CNS. T-cell lymphomas with low-grade histological features may be associated with a more favourable outcome than high-grade T-cell lymphomas {15725082}. In one series, 20% of patients with PTCL-NOS were alive without lymphoma at last follow-up, whereas 40% were alive with disease and 40% had died of the disease {26379152}. Methotrexate-based chemotherapy is the most common treatment regimen used. In a cohort of 45 patients with primary CNS lymphoma of T-cell origin, the median progression-free survival and overall survival were 22 and 25 months, respectively {15800313}.

The prognosis of patients with extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma of the CNS is poor, and most patients experience rapidly progressive disease. Median survival is approximately 6 months (range: 1–18 months) {20845062; 24419127; 28342197}. Long-term survival is rare {28342197}. Because primary CNS NK/T-cell lymphomas are rare, no standard treatment protocol exists. Methotrexate-based chemotherapy may be beneficial {24419127}.
